note: Wren Phonics teacher handbook. Criteria and routines text is Wren’s own; the pronunciation and alternatives guides are generated from the GPC and alternatives catalogs; the model lesson and first-two-weeks walkthrough follow the generated lesson data.

criteria.text: Constitute a complete programme, with fidelity to its own teaching framework throughout.
criteria.meets: One week-by-week sequence runs through Reception and Year 1; every lesson, assessment and printable in this pack is generated from it. Year 2 is an outline only, not yet planned week by week.

criteria.text: Treat systematic synthetic phonics as the prime approach to decoding print.
criteria.meets: No picture-guessing and no words to learn "by sight" — including the characters' names. A name appears in a book only once its sounds have been taught (Pip after i); Olive is taught as a tricky word, with its silent e as the tricky part, until 've' is taught in Year 1.

criteria.text: Start early in Reception and provide a route to the Year 1 Phonics Screening Check and KS1 word-reading expectations.
criteria.meets: Teaching starts Reception Autumn 1 Week 2; a PSC-review block sits in Year 1 Summer 1. Year 2 has an outline (review, the Year 2 common exception words and spelling) rather than week-by-week plans.

criteria.text: Be built for daily teaching sessions, in a clearly defined, incremental GPC sequence.
criteria.meets: A lesson card for every school day, every week, generated from the same fixed GPC order as the schedule.

criteria.text: Begin with a defined set of GPCs that unlock many early words.
criteria.meets: Reception opens with s, a, t, p, i, n, m, d: eight common sounds that make many short words in the first three weeks.

criteria.text: Progress from simple to complex, cumulatively covering all the major GPCs.
criteria.meets: Phase 2 → 3 → 4 (words with adjacent consonants — no new sounds) → 5 (new graphemes, including the Year 1 spellings tch, ve and are) → 5b (alternative pronunciations and spellings, including ear as in bear) → 6 (suffixes and prefixes). This covers the GPCs in the National Curriculum Year 1 spelling appendix; Year 2 spellings such as ey in key are left to Year 2.

criteria.text: Teach blending (synthesising) phonemes left to right through the whole word.
criteria.meets: Every "New sound" and "Have a go" box blends left to right; the dot/bar sound-button convention is used throughout print and slides.

criteria.text: Teach segmenting for spelling as the reverse of blending.
criteria.meets: Every lesson pairs its reading words with spelling/dictation words built from the same sounds.

criteria.text: Give practice applying known GPCs through dictation of sounds, words and sentences.
criteria.meets: Every lesson’s "Use it" box carries a dictation item from that week’s checked word bank, using only GPCs and tricky words already taught.

criteria.text: Teach common-exception ("tricky") words appropriate to progress.
criteria.meets: Tricky words are scheduled week by week (one to three a week), each with a "what’s tricky here" tip. Words the lessons use from the start (a, is, the, put, his, has, of, as) are taught in Reception. put, push, pull and full are on the National Curriculum Year 1 list: put is a Reception tricky word, and push, pull and full are taught as decodable words in Year 1, when u as /oo/ is taught.

criteria.text: Support correct letter formation, moving on to writing words and simple sentences.
criteria.meets: A formation cue with a clear start and finish point for every letter, lower case and capital (pronunciation guide below and the handwriting guide), plus the handwriting-expectations section in this handbook.

criteria.text: Be built around direct teaching with extensive interaction, including guidance for online delivery.
criteria.meets: Warm up → New sound → Have a go → Use it on every lesson card; see "Online delivery" below for live/recorded adaptation.

criteria.text: Provide sufficient decodable reading material closely matched to the taught code.
criteria.meets: Not yet met for Year 1. 93 books are illustrated and published, each placed in the first week every word in it can be read (61 matched to Reception weeks, 14 to Year 1 weeks). 213 books are written in all; the rest are waiting for illustration, and 50 more are planned. Until they are published, Year 1 needs other books that match this sequence (DfE Note 7).

criteria.text: Provide guidance so children practise and apply the core phonics taught, with SEND adaptations.
criteria.meets: "Have a go" and "Use it" on every lesson; see "SEND" below for adapting the same lesson, not a different programme.

criteria.text: Allow progress to be assessed, with a route for those at risk of falling behind.
criteria.meets: "Same-day boost" on every lesson card; a check for each of the 12 half-terms, Year 1 fluency checks and Phonics Screening Check practice; see "Assessment" below.

criteria.text: Provide full guidance and training for teachers.
criteria.meets: Not yet met for schools using the free materials: this handbook and the lesson-plan and slide packs are the only guidance. A staff course exists inside Wren, but there is no training for outside schools yet.

terminology.def: The smallest unit of SOUND in speech — what you hear, not what you see written down. The word "cat" has three phonemes: /c/ /a/ /t/.
The written letter or letters used to show a phoneme. One phoneme can be spelled with different graphemes (/ai/ can be "ai", "ay" or "a-e").
Two letters making one phoneme with another letter between them (e.g. the "a" and silent "e" in "cake" — a-e).
Pulling individual phonemes together, left to right, to read a whole word.
Splitting a spoken word into its individual phonemes to spell it — the reverse of blending.
A common word that cannot yet be fully decoded with the GPCs taught so far (also called a common-exception word).
Two or three consonant sounds said one after another with no vowel between them (e.g. the "s" and "t" in "stop") — Phase 4’s whole focus; always shown as separate sounds, never one grapheme card.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long hiss you can hold for as long as you like — 'sssss', not 'suh'. Don't let a vowel sneak onto the end.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top right. Curve up and round to the left, then across and back round to the right, and round to the left at the bottom. Finish at the bottom left.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, flat sound made with the mouth open wide — 'a' as in 'cat', not the long letter name.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top right of a small round shape. Curve round to the left and all the way back up to where you started, then go straight down without lifting. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A quick, light tap of the tongue behind the top teeth — 't', not 'tuh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start a little above the small letters. Pull straight down and finish on the line with a small curve to the right. Lift, then draw a short line across at the top of the small letters, from left to right.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A little puff of air as closed lips pop open — 'p', not 'puh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down below the line, go back up the same line, then curve round to the right and back. Finish where the curve meets the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, quick sound — 'i' as in 'sit', not the long letter name 'eye'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down and finish on the line. Lift, and add a dot above.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A gentle hum through the nose with the tongue behind the top teeth — 'n', not 'nuh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down, go back up the same line, then over in a hump and down. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A closed-lip hum held for a moment — 'mmm', not 'muh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down, go back up, over in a hump and down, back up and over in a second hump and down. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A firm, quick tap of the tongue just behind the top teeth — 'd', not 'duh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top right of a small round shape. Curve round to the left and back up to where you started, keep going straight up to make a tall line, then come straight back down it without lifting. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A soft sound made at the back of the throat — 'g' as in 'got', not 'guh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top right of a small round shape. Curve round to the left and back up to where you started, then go straight down below the line and curl round to the left. Finish below the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, round sound made with rounded lips — 'o' as in 'dog', not the long letter name.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top. Curve round to the left, down, round the bottom and back up. Finish where you started, closing the circle.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, sharp sound from the back of the throat — 'c' as in 'cat', not 'cuh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top right. Curve up, over to the left, round and down. Finish at the bottom right, leaving the c open.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: The same sharp sound as 'c' — a quick, short 'k', not 'kuh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line and pull straight down. Finish on the line. Lift, start at the top right of the small letters, slant in to touch the tall line, then slant out. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one sharp sound — 'ck' says exactly the same as 'k', usually at the end of short words.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'c', then 'k', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, flat sound — 'e' as in 'egg', not the long letter name.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start on the left, halfway up the small letters. Go straight across to the right, then curve up, over and round to the left and along the bottom. Finish at the bottom right.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, quick sound from the middle of the mouth — 'u' as in 'sun', not 'yoo'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull down, curve round the bottom and up to the top, then straight back down. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A growly sound you can hold, 'rrr', with the tongue pulled back and not touching the roof of the mouth — not rolled, and not 'ruh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down, go back up the same line, then curve over to the right. Finish just past the top of the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A soft breath out with no sound from the throat — just breathe out 'h', don't add 'huh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line. Pull straight down, go back up part of the way, then over in a hump and down. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, bouncy sound with closed lips popping open — 'b', not 'buh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line. Pull straight down, go back up part of the way, then curve round to the right and back. Finish at the bottom of the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, steady hiss made with the top teeth resting on the bottom lip — 'ffff', not 'fuh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start a little below the top, on the right. Curve up and over to the left, then pull straight down. Finish on the line. Lift, then draw a short line across at the top of the small letters, from left to right.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one long sound — 'ff' says exactly the same steady hiss as single 'f'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'f' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A clear, light sound with the tongue tip touching just behind the top teeth — 'l', not 'luh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of a tall line. Pull straight down. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one clear sound — 'll' says exactly the same as single 'l', often at the end of short words.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'l' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Two letters, one long hiss — 'ss' says exactly the same as single 's', often at the end of short words.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 's' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Pure sound only, e.g. 'j-j-j' not 'juh' — keep it short and bouncy, no vowel on the end.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down below the line and curl round to the left. Finish below the line. Lift, and add a dot above.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A buzzy, continuous sound — top teeth rest gently on bottom lip and you can hold it, 'vvvv', don't add 'uh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters. Slant down to a point on the line, then slant up to the right. Finish at the top right.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Round your lips into a small circle before you start, then open them as you say 'w' — quick and rounded, not stretched.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters. Slant down to a point, up to the middle, down to a second point, then up. Finish at the top right.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is two sounds squashed together, 'k' then 's' — say them fast, one after the other: ks.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters and slant down to the right. Finish on the line. Lift, start at the top right and slant down to the left, crossing the first line. Finish on the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A quick sound made at the front of the mouth, 'y-y-y' — don't turn it into 'yuh'.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters and slant down to the right, to the line. Lift, start at the top right and slant down to the left, through the first line and on below it. Finish below the line.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A buzzing sound you can hold, 'zzzz' — feel it tickle your lips, don't add 'uh' on the end.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Start at the top left of the small letters. Go straight across to the right, slant down to the bottom left, then straight across to the right. Finish at the bottom right.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Still just one buzzing 'zzzz' sound even though it's written with two letters — hold it, don't say it twice.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'z' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Two sounds squashed together, 'k' then 'w' — say them fast as one: kw. These two letters are never split up.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'q': start at the top right of a small round shape, curve round to the left and back up, then pull straight down below the line and finish there. Then write 'u' close beside it. 'q' is always followed by 'u'.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: One quick sound made together, 'ch' — like a small sneeze, don't say 'c' and 'h' apart.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'c', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A soft, quiet sound you can hold, 'shhh' — like asking for quiet, no vowel added on the end.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 's', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Pop your tongue tip gently between your teeth and blow, 'th' — it can sound soft (thin) or buzzy (that), practise both.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 't', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A hum made at the back of the mouth, 'ng' — like the end of 'sing', hold it and feel your nose buzz slightly.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'n', then 'g', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, gliding sound, 'ai' as in 'rain' — let it stretch, it slides from one shape to another.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'i', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, stretched sound, 'ee' as in 'tree' — smile as you say it and hold it for a full breath.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'e' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long gliding sound, 'igh' as in 'night' — three letters, one sound, glide from a wide mouth to a smile.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'i', then 'g', then 'h', close together — three letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, rounded sound, 'oa' as in 'boat' — round your lips into an O shape and let it glide.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'a', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, deep sound, 'oo' as in 'moon' — round your lips small and hold it, this is the LONG version of oo.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o' twice, close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, light sound, 'oo' as in 'book' — quick and soft, this is the SHORT version, different from the long 'oo' in 'moon'. The two 'oo' sounds are easy to mix up: one holds long (moon), this one is quick and clipped (book).
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o' twice, close together, just like the long 'oo' — the letters are exactly the same, only the sound is different.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, open sound, 'ar' as in 'car' — open your mouth wide and let it drop back, hold it for a moment.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, rounded sound, 'or' as in 'for' — round your lips more than 'ar' and hold it steady.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A long, low sound made in the middle of the mouth, 'ur' as in 'burn' — lips slightly rounded, hold it steady like a purr.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'u', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A loud, gliding sound, 'ow' as in 'cow' — start wide and glide down, like a little yelp of surprise.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'w', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A short, sharp gliding sound, 'oi' as in 'coin' — start rounded and glide quickly to a smile, like calling out.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'i', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A gliding sound, 'ear' as in 'hear' — start short and glide gently towards 'uh', like leaning in to listen.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'a', then 'r', close together — three letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A gliding sound, 'air' as in 'chair' — start open and glide gently towards 'uh', let your voice float.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'i', then 'r', close together — three letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: A gliding sound, 'ure' as in 'sure' — lips rounded to start, gliding gently towards 'uh', soft and short.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'u', then 'r', then 'e', close together — three letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: 'er' as in 'her' and 'fern' — a steady sound like 'ur'. At the end of a longer word, as in 'hammer', it is lighter and quicker.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ai' in rain — 'ay' is usually used at the end of a word, like day and play.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'y', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ow' in cow — 'ou' usually appears in the middle of a word.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'u', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'igh' in night — 'ie' often appears at the end of a word.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'i', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ee' in tree — 'ea' is very common in the middle of words.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'a', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oi' in coin — 'oy' is usually used at the end of a word.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'y', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ur' in burn — 'ir' often appears in the middle of a word, right inside the word 'bird' itself.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'i', then 'r', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oo' in moon — 'ue' usually appears at the end of a word.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'u', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'or' in for — 'aw' usually appears at the end of a word.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'w', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Bouncy (clipped, said once, quickly)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Another way to write the /ch/ sound children already know from 'chip' — the t is silent. 'tch' comes straight after a short vowel at the end of a word: catch, fetch, kitchen. (Common exceptions: rich, which, much, such.)
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 't', then 'c', then 'h', close together — three letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'w' in web — the 'h' stays silent and mostly tags along in question words.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'w', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'f' in fan — 'ph' often appears in longer, more grown-up words.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'p', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: The /v/ sound children already know from 'van'. English words hardly ever end in the letter v, so when a word ends with a /v/ sound, an e is added after the v and makes no sound: give, live, have, sleeve.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'v', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oo' in moon — 'ew' usually appears at the end of a word.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'e', then 'w', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oa' in boat — 'oe' is a less common ending used in only a handful of words.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'o', then 'e', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'or' in for and 'aw' in saw — 'au' usually appears in the middle of a word.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'u', close together — two letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ai' in rain and 'ay' in day — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'a', then a consonant in the middle, then 'e' right at the end — like cake, where 'a' and 'e' are two ends of a bridge with 'k' standing on it.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: Another way to write the /air/ sound children already know from 'chair'. Say it the same way as 'air': care, share, scared.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: Write 'a', then 'r', then 'e', close together — three letters, one sound.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ee' in tree and 'ea' in tea — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'e', then a consonant, then 'e' again at the end — like these, where the two 'e's sit at opposite ends holding the middle letters between them.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'igh' in night and 'ie' in tie — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'i' with its dot, then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like time, where 'i' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letters like two stars at opposite ends of the sky.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oa' in boat and 'oe' in toe — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'o', then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like home, where 'o' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letter like two ends of the same nest.

pronunciation_guide.stretch_or_bounce: Stretchy (held for as long as you like)
pronunciation_guide.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'oo' in moon (and sometimes sounds like 'you', as in cube) — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
pronunciation_guide.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'u', then a consonant, then 'e' at the end — like cube, where 'u' and 'e' sit either side of the middle letter like two ends of the same tune.

alternatives_guide.teaching_note: At the end of a short word, 'y' can say the same sound as 'igh' in 'light'. Try it in: my, by, fly, cry, try, shy.

alternatives_guide.taught_as: /y/ as in yes, yak, yellow; also /igh/ as in my, fly
alternatives_guide.teaching_note: At the end of a LONGER word, 'y' usually says /ee/ instead. Compare a short word ('my') with a longer one ('happy') to hear the difference.
After a 'w', 'a' can say /o/ instead of its usual short sound. Listen for it in: was, what, want, wash, wasp, swan.
On its own at the end of a tiny word, 'e' can say its long name-sound /ee/. Try: he, me, she, be, we.
Before 'nd', 'i' often says its long name-sound /igh/ instead of the short sound. Try: find, mind, kind, behind, blind.
On its own at the end of a word, 'o' can say its long name-sound /oa/. Try: go, no, so, zero.

alternatives_guide.taught_as: /o/ as in dog, hot, top; also /oa/ as in go, no
alternatives_guide.teaching_note: Sometimes 'o' says /u/ instead of either of its other sounds — these just have to be heard and remembered. Try: son, mother, come, love, some.
After certain letters, 'u' can say the short /oo/ sound instead. Try: put, full, pull, push, bull.

alternatives_guide.taught_as: /u/ as in sun, cup, mud; also /oo/ as in put, full
alternatives_guide.teaching_note: At the start of some words, 'u' says /yoo/ — like the letter's own name. Try: unicorn, unit, uniform, universe.
Before 'e', 'i' or 'y', 'c' usually says /s/ instead of /k/. Try: cent, city, ice, fence, pencil.
Before 'e', 'i' or 'y', 'g' can say /j/ instead of /g/. Try: giant, gem, cage, stage.
In some words (often borrowed from other languages), 'ch' says /k/ instead. Try: school, chorus, echo, Christmas, stomach.

alternatives_guide.taught_as: /ch/ as in chip, chat, much; also /k/ as in school
alternatives_guide.teaching_note: In a few other borrowed words, 'ch' says /sh/ instead. Try: chef, machine, chalet, moustache.
The same two letters 'ow' can also say /oa/, like in 'go'. Try: snow, grow, own, slow, window.
In the middle of some words, 'ie' says /ee/ instead of /igh/. Try: field, chief, thief, shield, believe.
In a group of words, 'ea' says the short sound /e/ instead of /ee/. Try: head, bread, spread, instead, breakfast.
In a few words, 'ou' says the long /oo/ sound instead. Try: soup, group, you, route, youth.

alternatives_guide.taught_as: /ow/ as in out, loud, round; also /oo/ as in soup, you
alternatives_guide.teaching_note: In another small group, 'ou' says the short /u/ sound. Try: young, touch, country, double, cousin.
In some words, 'ear' says /er/ instead of /ear/ — there's no simple rule for which, so these are best learned as a small group. Try: earn, learn, early, pearl, heard.

alternatives_guide.taught_as: /ear/ as in hear, year, dear; also /er/ as in learn, early
alternatives_guide.teaching_note: 'ear' can also say /air/, the same sound as in 'chair' — in a small set of everyday words: bear, pear, wear, tear (as in tear a page). Read the word both ways and choose the one that makes sense.
Straight after a 'w', 'or' says /er/ instead of /or/. Try: word, work, world, worm, worth.
Four letters, one sound — 'eigh' says /ai/, the same sound already known from 'rain' and 'day'.
Without the silent 'gh', 'ei' can say the same /ai/ sound on its own.
At the end of a word, 'ey' most often says /ee/ (like 'key' or 'monkey'). In a smaller group of words it says /ai/ instead (like 'they' or 'grey') — point out both when they come up.
At the end of a word, 'ore' says /or/ — the same sound already known from 'for', spelled with a silent 'e' on the end.
A small group of words spell /or/ with 'oor' instead.
Another way to spell /or/ — say it as /or/, not as the 'ou' sound in 'out'.

phase4_structures.label: CVCC words
phase4_structures.title: Two consonant sounds together at the end
phase4_structures.explanation: Words that end with two consonant sounds, like tent and milk. Say every sound, then blend: t-e-n-t, tent. Do not squash the last two sounds into one.

phase4_structures.label: CCVC words
phase4_structures.title: Two consonant sounds together at the start
phase4_structures.explanation: Words that start with two consonant sounds, like stop and frog. Say every sound, then blend: s-t-o-p, stop. For a sound you can hold (s, f, l), hold it and slide into the next one.

phase4_structures.label: CCVCC words
phase4_structures.title: Two consonant sounds at the start and two at the end
phase4_structures.explanation: Both skills in one word: crisp, trust, frost. Say every sound, left to right, then blend.

phase4_structures.label: Two-syllable words
phase4_structures.title: Longer words with two syllables
phase4_structures.explanation: Clap the two beats first (sand-pit), read each chunk sound by sound, then put the chunks together.

phase4_structures.label: With sh, ch, th and ng
phase4_structures.title: Adjacent consonants in words with sh, ch, th or ng
phase4_structures.explanation: A digraph is still one sound: in chest, ch is one sound and s-t are two. Count the sounds, then blend: ch-e-s-t, four sounds.

phase4_structures.label: With long vowel sounds
phase4_structures.title: Adjacent consonants in words with long vowel sounds
phase4_structures.explanation: The vowel digraph is one sound: tr-ai-n is four sounds, t-r-ai-n. Spot the digraph first, then blend every sound.

phase4_structures.label: Three consonants together
phase4_structures.title: Three consonant sounds together
phase4_structures.explanation: Some words start with three consonant sounds: s-t-r in strap, s-p-l in split. Each is its own sound; say all three, then blend.

phase4_structures.label: Longer and compound words
phase4_structures.title: Longer words and compound words
phase4_structures.explanation: Two short words joined together (farm + yard) or a longer word in two beats. Find the chunks, read each one, then blend them together.

daily_routine.intro: Every Wren Phonics lesson follows the same four-part shape, so children always know what is coming. Timing grows across the year: around 10 minutes a day in the first days of Reception, building to about 30 minutes for the daily lesson by the end of Reception and through Year 1. With reading practice, handwriting and dictation, that adds up to the "about an hour a day, maybe split into different sessions" the Reading Framework (July 2023, p.50) expects by the end of Reception. The schedule does not fix a minute-by-minute timetable, so use a pace that keeps every child engaged rather than a stopwatch.
parts: Revisit recently-taught graphemes on flashcards and orally blend a handful of known words — quick, no new learning, just keeping everything already taught fast and automatic.

Teach the day’s new grapheme (or alternative/suffix/prefix) directly: say it, show its mnemonic and formation, model it in words with sound buttons. Multi-sensory — voice, picture and action together. In Phase 4 there are no new sounds: this part introduces the week’s new kind of word instead (for example CVCC words, with two consonant sounds at the end).
Children read and spell words using the new content plus everything already known, including this week’s tricky word where there is one. Mini-whiteboards or books, not finished worksheets.
Apply it for real: read a short caption or phrase aloud, then write a dictated sentence. This is the moment reading and spelling meet connected text.

routine_worked_examples.Warm up: Reception, Autumn 1, Week 2, Wednesday: by this point the class knows "s" (Monday) and "a" (Tuesday) but not yet "t". Flashcard revisit shows "s" then "a"; children say each sound back. Two sounds cannot make a printed word yet, so blending stays oral: the adult says a familiar word sound by sound ("s‑u‑n", "m‑a‑t") and children blend it purely by ear, with no print in sight. This is deliberately light: nothing new, just keeping yesterday's learning fast and automatic before today's new sound.
routine_worked_examples.New sound: Same lesson, straight after the warm up: "t" is introduced as /t/ — "a quick, light tap of the tongue behind the top teeth — 't', not 'tuh'" (the exact wording this programme's own catalog gives for this grapheme). The mnemonic is Tolly the feather, who "taps gently on the twig every time the wind blows — 't, t, t'"; the formation cue starts a little above the small letters, pulls straight down and finishes on the line with a small curve, then a short line across from left to right; the action taps one fingertip on the back of the other hand twice. Only once "s" and "a" are ALSO known can a real model word use "t" — here "sat" and "at", both re-checked against exactly what has been taught up to and including today, not the whole week's end state.
routine_worked_examples.Have a go: Children read "sat" and "at" aloud, pointing under each sound button (s·a·t, a·t) and blending left to right, then write the same two words from dictation, segmenting them sound by sound. No nonsense words happen to fit this particular day (the taught set is still thin this early in the week) — that is expected, not a gap, and nothing forces a nonsense word in before one can honestly be made from taught sounds alone.
routine_worked_examples.Use it: There is no caption yet: with only s, a and t known, no sentence can be made from taught sounds — not even one with a character's name, because Pip needs i, which is taught next week. So Use it is dictation of the single word "at", which is entirely normal in the first fortnight; captions start on Thursday ("a tap") once p is known, and the first books (Pip Sat and Pip and the Tin) come in Week 3, when every word in them, Pip included, can be sounded out.

call_and_response: Every new sound, every model word and every Have a go item is said chorally first ("my turn, then everyone") before any child reads alone — this keeps every child actively responding, not just the fastest hands, and gives the adult an instant check of who is and is not saying it correctly. Keep the response snappy: say it once clearly, children echo it once, move on.
blend_segment_routine: Reading (blending): point under each sound button left to right, say each sound once, then run your finger under the whole word and blend the sounds together into the word, at normal speaking speed — never sound-by-sound-by-sound as a chant with no blend at the end.

Spelling (segmenting): say the whole word once, then say each sound in it in order, writing (or pointing to) the matching grapheme for each one as you go — this is blending in reverse, and every child should be able to tell you that.

Oral blending/segmenting (no print needed) comes first for brand-new learners and stays useful throughout: say a word sound by sound and have children blend it purely by ear, or say a whole word and have them segment it purely by ear, with no letters in sight.
tricky_word_routine: Read it first: show the whole word, read it together, and ask which part is the "tricky" bit — the part that does not sound the way its letters usually do.
Name the tricky part out loud (e.g. "the "ay" in "said" sounds like "e", not its usual sound") using that word’s own tip in the pronunciation guide/bank data.
Spell it after reading it, never before. Sound out the parts that follow the known sounds, point to the tricky part, and practise until the whole word is quick.
Keep a running tricky-word display as the term goes on; a 30-second daily flash through words-so-far keeps old ones fast, which matters more than drilling the newest one alone.
dictation_routine: Say the whole sentence (or word) once, normally, before anyone writes anything.
Say it again in short chunks a child can hold in working memory, pausing to let children segment and write each chunk.
Every word in a Wren dictation item uses only GPCs and tricky words already taught that week or earlier — never ahead of the schedule.
Re-read the finished sentence together and check it reads back correctly — this catches a missed word faster than checking spellings letter by letter.

model_lesson_transcript.intro: A full lesson script, start to finish, for the SAME real day used in the worked examples above (Reception, Autumn 1, Week 2, Wednesday — the day "t" is taught). Every word a child reads or writes here comes from that day's checked lesson data. Adjust your own wording and pacing; this is a worked example of the SHAPE, not a script to recite verbatim.
lines: Let's warm up our ears and our sounds. Watch my card.
Good. Now ears only, no cards: s — u — n. Blend it for me.
Lovely blending. One more: m — a — t.
We're going to learn a brand new sound today. It's a little tap sound. Watch Tolly the feather — he taps gently on the twig every time the wind blows. T, t, t.
(tap one fingertip on the back of the other hand, twice) "t, t"

Nice and light — a quick little tap of your tongue behind your top teeth. Not "tuh", just "t". Let's write it: one tall line down, like the twig, then a short line across near the top, like Tolly tapping it. In the air with me.
Now watch — I'm going to put sounds together: s... a... t. (points under each sound button) Blend them with me, all the way through.
We made a real word! What about this one — a... t?
Your turn — whiteboards out. Write "sat" for me. Say it, then say each sound as you write it.
(write s-a-t, saying each sound while writing)
Show me your boards... lovely. Last job — dictation. I'm going to say a word, and you write it: "at". Say it, segment it, write it.
Let's read it back together: a-t...

Brilliant. Next week we learn i, and then we can read a whole book about Pip — we'll be able to sound out his name, p-i-p. Anyone who wants Tolly's tap sound again gets it in our small group straight after lunch.

common_errors.mistake: Adding a vowel onto a pure consonant sound ("tuh", "muh", "buh" instead of "t", "m", "b").
common_errors.why: It distorts blending — a child trying to blend "c‑uh‑a‑t" hears four sounds, not three, and "cuhat" is not a word they can recognise as "cat".
common_errors.fix: Say the sound alone, clipped and quick for a bouncy sound ("t" not "tuh"), held for a stretchy one ("mmm" not "muh"). Check your own pronunciation against this handbook's pronunciation guide before teaching a new sound for the first time.

common_errors.mistake: Sounding out a word sound-by-sound with no final blend ("s... a... t" and stopping, with no "sat" at the end).
common_errors.why: Segmenting without blending leaves a child able to name the sounds but not read the word — the whole point of the final blend is pulling the sounds into real, running speech.
common_errors.fix: Always finish by running a finger smoothly under the whole word and saying it at normal speed: "s‑a‑t... sat." Model the blend yourself before asking a child to do it alone.

common_errors.mistake: Asking a child to sound out a tricky word ("th‑e" for "the").
common_errors.why: A tricky word contains a GPC that is unusual or not yet taught — sounding it out produces the wrong word and teaches an incorrect decoding habit for exactly the words where it matters most.
common_errors.fix: Show the whole word, read it together, name the tricky part out loud using that word's own tip, then practise spelling it from memory — read-then-spell, never sound-by-sound.

common_errors.mistake: Telling children a character's name "by sight" instead of letting them sound it out.
common_errors.why: Names are words like any other. Wren Phonics only uses a name once its sounds have been taught (Pip after i; Ned, Fig, Moss and Nell in Autumn 2), so children can read it the same way they read everything else. The DfE asks programmes not to give children words to learn as whole shapes "by sight".
common_errors.fix: Point under the sound buttons and blend the name: p-i-p, Pip. Olive is the one exception in Reception: teach it as a tricky word — sound out O-l-i-v and point out the silent e — until 've' is taught in Year 1.

common_errors.mistake: Introducing a brand-new GPC before the warm-up has checked what is already secure.
common_errors.why: New content lands on top of shaky foundations, and the same gap resurfaces lesson after lesson instead of being caught and fixed the same day.
common_errors.fix: Never skip the warm up, even when short on time — a 90-second flashcard check is what tells you whether yesterday's learning is actually secure enough to build on today.

common_errors.mistake: Treating an alternative pronunciation or spelling (e.g. "ow" in "cow" vs "ow" in "snow") as if it were a brand new letter to learn from scratch.
common_errors.why: The grapheme itself is already known — what's new is only the second sound it can make. Teaching it as if nothing were known yet wastes the lesson and can confuse a child who correctly remembers the FIRST sound.
common_errors.fix: Say explicitly "you already know 'ow' says /ow/ as in 'cow' — today we're learning it can ALSO say /oa/, like in 'snow'", and model words with both the old and new reading side by side.

common_errors.mistake: Treating adjacent consonants (s and t in "stop", n and d in "hand") as one new fused sound, with its own grapheme card.
common_errors.why: They are two sounds children already know. Presenting them as one new sound ("/st/") makes the separate sounds harder to hear later for spelling — the DfE asks for /s/+/p/+/l/, not /spl/.
common_errors.fix: Never make a grapheme card for a pair of consonants. Phase 4 is planned by kind of word (CVCC, then CCVC, then longer words): point under every sound button, say every sound, then blend — s-t-o-p, stop.

common_errors.mistake: Running dictation as "write this down" with no re-read at the end.
common_errors.why: A child can mishear or drop a word entirely and never find out, because nobody checked the finished sentence actually says what it was meant to say.
common_errors.fix: Always read the finished sentence back together and ask "does that say what I asked for?" before moving on — this catches a missed or wrong word far faster than checking spelling letter by letter.

common_errors.mistake: Naming letters ("ess", "tee", "em") instead of sounds during a phonics lesson.
common_errors.why: Letter NAMES are a different, later skill (useful for alphabetical order, spelling aloud) — mixing them into blending and segmenting teaches two systems at once and slows both down.
common_errors.fix: Stick to sounds throughout every phonics lesson ("s", "t", "m", not "ess", "tee", "em"). Letter names can be taught separately, once blending and segmenting with sounds is secure.

common_errors.mistake: Forcing a word into a lesson because it "should" be ready, when it does not actually pass the week's own taught set.
common_errors.why: A word that only looks right (e.g. assuming "tap" is fine on the day "t" is introduced, when "p" is not taught until the following day) teaches a child to decode using a letter they have not actually been taught — it works today only because they half-guessed.
common_errors.fix: Trust the generated lesson data's own day-by-day word lists rather than reaching for a word that "feels" about right — if a word is not listed for that specific day, it has not yet been checked as decodable with what that day has actually taught.

common_errors.mistake: Skipping the "same-day boost" because the lesson overran and moving straight on to tomorrow's new content regardless.
common_errors.why: A gap left unfixed on the day it appears tends to compound — tomorrow's new sound is taught assuming today's is secure, so a child who needed the boost and didn't get it starts the next day already behind.
common_errors.fix: Protect a short same-day slot even on a tight day — a few focused minutes 1:1 or in a small group is enough; it does not need to be the full lesson again.

common_errors.mistake: Reading a decodable book TO a child instead of having them decode it, "to save time".
common_errors.why: It silently swaps the skill being practised — a book session that is really a listening session does not give the independent decoding practice the matched book exists for.
common_errors.fix: Let the child do the decoding, with support only where they genuinely get stuck — a slower, child-led read is more valuable here than a fast, adult-led one.

handwriting: Correct posture and a comfortable tripod pencil grip come before accuracy — do not let a wobbly grip become a habit while chasing neat letters.
Every formation cue in this handbook gives a clear start point and finish point for each grapheme; teach those points explicitly, every time, from the very first letter.
No lead-in or joining strokes at this stage (these are not taught until letters are secure) — print only, matching every piece of text children are given to read.

Writing moves from forming single graphemes, to words made of taught GPCs, to simple sentences using taught GPCs and tricky words — in that order, never skipping ahead to independent writing before the sounds inside it have been taught.
Mini-whiteboards are for quick practice only — a child’s actual progress (what they can securely write) belongs in their own book or a dated written record, not only on a wipeable surface.
reading_practice_overview: Alongside daily phonics lessons, children read their matched decodable book in small reading-practice sessions, re-reading the same book two or three times across the week for growing fluency rather than moving straight to a new one each time (the standard "practice read, then two further reads" shape most SSP programmes use). Grouping, timing and the exact session structure for Wren Phonics reading-practice sessions are set out in full in the reading-practice guide and session cards — this handbook covers only how reading practice fits around the daily lesson above.
assessment_overview: Every half-term’s Week 6 is a built-in review-and-assessment week (see the progression overview) — check every GPC, alternative and tricky word taught that half-term against the schedule, not just the newest ones.
Keep an individual record for each child, not only a whole-group tick list — the Reading Framework is explicit that group-only records miss children who are falling behind quietly.
Assess a new child joining mid-year immediately against the schedule, starting their lessons at the point their assessment actually shows, not at their year group’s current week by default.

The Year 1 Summer 1 PSC-review block (see the progression overview) exists to build confidence with the Check’s own untimed, one-to-one format (four words to a page) — never drill a wall of pseudo-words to "prepare"; real practice at the right level does more.

first_two_weeks.intro: What the very first two weeks of Reception actually look like, lesson by lesson, taken directly from this programme's own generated schedule and lesson data (Reception, Autumn 1, Weeks 1 and 2) — not a general description, the real content a Reception class will see.

week1.heading: Week 1 — settling in (no letters yet)
week1.note: Every day this week is Phase 1 listening and speaking — tuning children's ears before a single grapheme is taught, while the class settles in. Ofsted does not expect phonics teaching in nursery, so many children arrive having done little of this; the Reading Framework's daily poems, rhymes and songs belong here too.
days: Monday
Listening Walk — a sound hunt basket and a "freeze and point" game outdoors or around the room, simply noticing and naming everyday sounds.
Tuesday
Instrument Sounds — guessing real and homemade instruments from sound alone, then a loud-and-quiet shaker march.
Wednesday
Body Percussion — a body-sound orchestra (clap, stamp, click, pat knees) and an echo-the-pattern game, using nothing but their own bodies.
Thursday
Rhythm & Rhyme — nursery rhymes and a rhyme-matching basket game, building a feel for a steady beat and for words that rhyme.
Friday

Review — revisit favourite games from the week (this week's review happens to spotlight Alliteration, listening for words that start the same) — still no letters, just an informal check of who is confidently joining in.

week2.heading: Week 2 — the first four letter sounds (s, a, t, p)
week2.note: Four common sounds that already make real words like "sat", "tap" and "pat". Note how thin the very first days necessarily are: Monday has no real-word practice at all (one sound alone cannot make a word), and Tuesday only has "a" — this is correct practice, not a shortfall. The worked example above walks through Wednesday ("t"), the first day with a real word to read and write. There is no matched book this week: the first books come in Week 3, when every word in them, including Pip's name, can be sounded out.
days: Monday

send_guidance: Every child learns to read through the same systematic synthetic phonics approach — Wren Phonics does not switch a struggling child to a different programme or strategy; it adapts delivery of this one.
Adapt by: smaller steps, more repetition, a slower pace, a quieter space with fewer distractions, and more 1:1 or small-group time — not by skipping content or changing the sequence.
Multi-sensory by default already helps many additional needs (voice, picture, movement together) — lean further into the action/formation cue for a child who needs a physical anchor for a sound.
Trial any adaptation with the specific child it is for before relying on it across a group — what helps one child with a particular need may not help another with a different one.

Phonics Screening Check: STA's 2026 administration guidance (section 5.2, on GOV.UK) allows adjustments that are normal classroom practice without asking permission — rest breaks (finishing on the same day), a modified font, font size or fewer words per page, coloured overlays, and Cued Speech or visual phonics to make answers clear. A child who uses sound buttons may mark them on a clean copy, but the adult must not mark them. Readers are not allowed. Check the current year's guidance; the SEND guide summarises it.

Wren Phonics does not use sand, shaving foam, paint or dough letters for phonics: the DfE validation guidance (Note 8) and the Reading Framework (2023, p.55) both warn that they take attention away from the letters. The SEND guide has alternatives, and guidance for speech sound difficulties, non-verbal children and AAC users, hearing and visual impairment, and the graduated approach.
eal_guidance: An EAL child learns English phonics the same way any child does — through this same sequence — but may need more oral language and vocabulary support around it, since a word may be unfamiliar in meaning even once it is correctly decoded.
Check understanding of a model word’s MEANING as well as its sounds: pre-teach the week’s key words with pictures or objects before the lesson, especially for the more abstract tricky words.

Some English sounds do not exist, or are not told apart, in a child’s home language, so expect these and give them extra listening and mouth-shape practice rather than treating them as errors. Common examples: /v/ and /w/ (vet, wet) for many speakers of Punjabi, Urdu, Hindi, Gujarati and Bengali; the two "th" sounds (thin, this), missing from many languages; /p/ and /b/ (pin, bin) for many Arabic speakers; short and long vowels (ship, sheep; full, fool) for speakers of languages with fewer vowel sounds, such as Polish or Spanish; and two or three consonants together (stop, splash), where speakers of languages without them may add a vowel ("is-top"). The standard reference is Swan and Smith, Learner English (2nd edition, 2001). Accent differences are fine; what matters is the right sound for each grapheme.

A new arrival in Year 1: assess them straight away with the placement check (the Reading Framework, p.59, says to assess new pupils immediately), start their phonics where the check shows, add a short daily Same-day boost, and give them matched books at that level, not their year group’s level.

Families: the Wren family guides are available in 30 languages. They were translated by computer and checked by a second, separate computer back-translation, not by native speakers, so ask a bilingual colleague or parent to look one over before you send it home. For a parent who does not read their home language, go through the guide’s key points in person with an interpreter, use the pictures, and show the pure sounds by saying them together.
Celebrate and use a child’s home language as a resource where you can (for example, noticing a sound that does or doesn’t exist in it) rather than treating it as something to work around.
Keep expectations for the phonics sequence itself unchanged — slow the support around it, not the code being taught.
online_delivery: Live online: keep the same four-part routine and the same call-and-response rhythm — ask specific children to respond by name in turn so the session stays interactive rather than becoming one-way.
Recorded: a recording supports the routine, it never replaces the teacher’s own live teaching of a new sound for the first time — use recordings for revisiting/practice, not first teaching.
Screen-share the same grapheme cards, word lists and sound buttons used in the room, so a child moving between in-person and online sessions sees identical materials.
Keep sessions short and the routine predictable — the same "what is coming next" structure that matters in the room matters even more on a screen, where attention is harder to hold.
organising_resources: Grapheme cards, word cards and this term’s matched decodable books should match the week being taught, not be a generic wall display built once for the year — swap them on as the schedule moves.
A quiet, low-distraction space for keep-up ("Same-day boost") sessions and 1:1 PSC-style practice, used consistently so children know what that space means.
Keep a visible, growing tricky-word and taught-sounds display that only ever adds — removing something before it is secure sends the wrong signal.
Store each half-term’s lesson-plan pack, matched books and bank word lists together so a cover teacher can pick up exactly where the class left off.

faqs.q: What if a child joins the class mid-term, already knowing some sounds?
faqs.a: Assess them against the schedule straight away rather than starting at week one by default — place their lessons at the point the assessment actually shows, and use "Same-day boost" sessions to fill any specific gaps the assessment finds, rather than re-teaching everything from scratch.

faqs.q: What if more than a handful of the class aren't secure with this week's sounds by Friday?
faqs.a: If close to a third or more of the group has the same gap, that is a signal to slow the WHOLE class's pace, not just run more 1:1 keep-up — re-teach the content properly before moving on, because the next week's new content assumes this week's is already secure.

A tricky word contains at least one GPC that is unusual or not yet taught (e.g. the "o" in "to" does not say its usual sound) — sounding it out the normal way would produce the wrong word. So children sound out the parts that do follow the sounds they know, then notice the tricky part and remember it, exactly as the "Teaching tricky words" routine above sets out.

faqs.q: Our setting has children with English as an additional language — do we teach phonics differently for them?
faqs.a: No — the phonics sequence itself stays exactly the same; what changes is the oral language and vocabulary support around it. See "EAL" below for specifics.

faqs.q: What if a child cannot do the formation/action for a sound because of a motor difficulty?
faqs.a: Keep the sound, mnemonic and voice elements exactly as taught, and adapt only the physical anchor — see "SEND" below; the goal is the same phonic knowledge by a different physical route, never a different programme.

faqs.q: Do we need to buy or print flashcards for every single grapheme before we start?
faqs.a: No — "Organising the classroom and resources" below is explicit that only THIS week's cards need to be out; build the display up as the schedule moves rather than printing the whole year up front.

faqs.q: A parent has asked why their child brings home such a short, simple book — shouldn't they be reading something longer by now?
faqs.a: The matched decodable book is deliberately limited to graphemes already taught — a book that "feels" more advanced would contain untaught code, forcing the child to guess rather than decode. Explain that matching, not difficulty for its own sake, is the point (see "Reading practice sessions" below).

faqs.q: What exactly counts as "practice" for a brand new sound if there aren't enough letters yet to make a real word?
faqs.a: Oral blending and sound recognition — saying the sound, hearing it in words you say aloud, practising its formation and action — is genuine, correct practice in its own right at this stage, not a placeholder for "real" practice; see the Warm-up and New-sound worked examples above for what this looks like on an actual early day.

faqs.q: How do we know a word is genuinely safe to use in a lesson, rather than just looking about right?
faqs.a: Every word in this programme's lesson data has already been checked, day by day, against exactly what has been taught up to and including that specific day — not the whole week's eventual total. Trust the generated lesson/bank data rather than judging a word by eye; see the final "Common errors" entry above for what can go wrong otherwise.

faqs.q: Why do some weeks have no new content at all?
faqs.a: Consolidation and review weeks are built into every half-term on purpose — a half-term that only ever added new content, with no week to secure it, would outrun what children can actually retain. These weeks re-practise, they do not pad.

faqs.q: Isn't the pace slow — only 26 sounds by Christmas?
faqs.a: It is a deliberate choice, and slower than several well-known programmes: every half-term has four teaching weeks, a consolidation week and a review week, so that no child is carried on before the code is secure. It has not yet been tested with a Reception class, and we will review it with pilot schools. If your whole class is secure, use the consolidation week for more reading of the matched books rather than moving on early: the books and word lists follow this order.

faqs.q: Why are put, push, pull and full not on the Year 1 tricky-word list?
faqs.a: They are on the National Curriculum Year 1 list. In Wren Phonics, put is taught as a tricky word in Reception, because the lessons use it from Autumn 2. push, pull and full are taught in Year 1 Spring 1 as decodable words, when children learn that u can also say /oo/ (as in book), so they are not tricky by then.

faqs.q: Is Wren Phonics a DfE-validated programme?
faqs.a: No. The DfE's validation rounds have closed, so no new programme can be validated. Wren Phonics is written to the 16 core criteria, but it has not been validated, and it has not yet been taught to a full Reception class. Schools supported by an English Hub are expected to use a validated programme. We are looking for pilot schools.

faqs.q: Can we use a different decodable book from a different scheme if we run out of matched Wren titles?
faqs.a: Only if it is fully matched to exactly what has been taught so far (DfE Note 7) — check it contains no untaught GPCs and no more than a couple of taught exception words before using it, and prefer waiting for the matched Wren title where you can.

faqs.q: A child can already read fluently when they start Reception — do they still do daily phonics?
faqs.a: Yes, but assess them properly first rather than assuming: place them at the point in the schedule their actual decoding (not just fluency from memorised books) shows, which may be well ahead of their peers. Daily phonics still matters for spelling and for any gaps a confident-sounding reader can quietly be covering over.

faqs.q: Is it a problem if a child's accent means a sound comes out slightly differently from the pronunciation guide?
faqs.a: No — the pronunciation guide and the Phonics Screening Check itself both allow for normal accent and speech variation; what matters is using the correct GPC and a genuinely PURE sound (no added vowel), not matching one specific accent exactly.

faqs.q: Why does a nonsense word need its own made-up-creature picture?
faqs.a: So a child knows at a glance it is not a real word and reads it purely by decoding rather than searching their memory for something that sounds similar — the same device the Phonics Screening Check itself uses for its pseudo-words.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the matched "reading practice" book and a "sharing" book sent home?
faqs.a: The reading-practice book is matched exactly to what has been taught, for the child to read independently; a sharing book is chosen more freely and read WITH an adult, for enjoyment rather than independent decoding — both matter, but only the first is assessed against the phonics schedule. Full detail sits in the reading-practice guide and session cards.
